```{r setup, include = FALSE}

    collapse = TRUE,

    fig.height = 4.5
```

```{r library}
library(semnova)
```

This vignette walks through everything the package currently does, using the
data that ships with it. Every feature that is implemented appears here; if a
function is exported and meant for users, you will find it below.

# What semnova is for

`semnova` fits repeated-measures ANOVA designs as structural equation models.
The advantage over a classical RM-ANOVA is that the dependent variable, and any
covariates, can be **latent**. They are measured by several indicators, with
measurement error taken out, rather than being manifest composites.

Under the hood, each design cell becomes a latent variable (`eta`), those are
transformed by a contrast matrix into contrast variables (`pi`), and every
effect you test is a general linear hypothesis on the `pi` layer. The maths is
in `vignette("glh", package = "semnova")`; you do not need it to use the
package.

# The example data

Two versions of a reading study ship with the package: `reading_manifest` (one
row per person and design cell) and `reading_latent` (the long form, with three
indicators per cell). The design is 3 (grade) x 2 (sentence type), within
subjects, with `sex` available as a between-subjects factor and `iq` as a
covariate.

```{r data}
str(reading_manifest[c("id", "grade", "sentence", "sex", "re_fix_time", "iq")])
table(reading_latent$indicator)
```

# A manifest within-subjects design

The simplest case: a single observed dependent variable, two crossed
within-subject factors. Give `semnova()` the long-format data, the case
identifier, the dependent variable, and the within factors.

`contrasts_arg` controls how each factor is coded. Anything R's own contrast
functions provide will do. Here we use sum-to-zero contrasts for both factors.

```{r manifest}
fit <- semnova(
    data = reading_manifest,
    id = "id",
    dv = "re_fix_time",
    withins = c("grade", "sentence"),
    contrasts_arg = list(grade = "contr.sum", sentence = "contr.sum")
)
```

Printing the fit gives you a description of the model and the ANOVA table: one
row per model term, tested as a general linear hypothesis.

```{r manifest-print}
fit
```

`anova()` on a single fit returns that table on its own, so you can work with
it programmatically. Given several fits it compares them as nested models
instead, which the invariance and covariance-structure sections below use.

```{r manifest-anova}
anova(fit)
```

`anova_table()` is the same thing under a name that says what it returns, for
when you would rather not go through the generic.

```{r manifest-anova-table}
identical(anova_table(fit), anova(fit))
```

`summary()` adds the estimates underneath each omnibus test.

```{r manifest-summary}
summary(fit)
```

# Adding a between-subjects factor

Naming a `betweens` factor fits a multigroup model, one group per level. It
extends the ANOVA table with the between-subject term and every interaction
involving it.

```{r between}
fit_between <- semnova(
    data = reading_manifest,
    id = "id",
    dv = "re_fix_time",
    withins = c("grade", "sentence"),
    betweens = "sex",
    contrasts_arg = list(
        grade = "contr.sum",
        sentence = "contr.sum",
        sex = "contr.treatment"
    )
)

anova_table(fit_between)
```

# A latent dependent variable

To make the dependent variable latent, point `indicator` at the column that says
which indicator each row holds. Every design cell is then measured by all of the
indicators, and the measurement model is estimated along with everything else.

We use two of the three available indicators here.

```{r latent}
reading_two <- reading_latent[reading_latent$indicator != "re_fix_time", ]

fit_latent <- semnova(
    data = reading_two,
    id = "id",
    dv = "dv",
    indicator = "indicator",
    withins = c("grade", "sentence"),
    contrasts_arg = list(grade = "contr.sum", sentence = "contr.sum")
)

anova_table(fit_latent)
```

Because a latent model is no longer saturated, global fit measures become
informative:

```{r latent-fit}
fit_measures(fit_latent)
```

# Covariates

`covariates` adds covariates. Each one enters as a predictor of every contrast
variable, so you get a main effect for the covariate plus its interactions with
the within-subject terms. Those interactions say whether the experimental
effects differ depending on the covariate.

```{r covariate}
fit_cov <- semnova(
    data = reading_two,
    id = "id",
    dv = "dv",
    indicator = "indicator",
    withins = c("grade", "sentence"),
    covariates = "iq",
    contrasts_arg = list(grade = "contr.sum", sentence = "contr.sum")
)

anova_table(fit_cov)
```

Covariates may be categorical. A factor is coded into contrast columns for
you, using `contrasts_arg` or `contr.treatment` by default. Its columns stay
**one term**, so a three-level covariate is a single effect with two degrees of
freedom rather than two separate effects:

```{r covariate-categorical}
reading_grouped <- reading_manifest
reading_grouped$iq_group <- cut(reading_grouped$iq, 3, labels = c("low", "mid", "high"))

fit_catcov <- semnova(
    data = reading_grouped,
    id = "id",
    dv = "re_fix_time",
    withins = c("grade", "sentence"),
    covariates = "iq_group",
    contrasts_arg = list(grade = "contr.sum", sentence = "contr.sum")
)

anova_table(fit_catcov)
```

`expand_categorical_covariates()` is the function that does the coding, should
you want the columns themselves:

```{r covariate-expand}
expand_categorical_covariates(reading_grouped, "iq_group", list())$terms
```

# Measurement invariance

With a latent dependent variable you can ask whether the measurement model holds
equally across measurement occasions. `invariance_within` takes the usual four
levels, each nested in the previous one.

```{r invariance}
invariance_fit <- function(level) {
    semnova(
        data = reading_two,
        id = "id",
        dv = "dv",
        indicator = "indicator",
        withins = c("grade", "sentence"),
        invariance_within = level,
        contrasts_arg = list(grade = "contr.sum", sentence = "contr.sum")
    )
}

configural <- invariance_fit("configural")
weak <- invariance_fit("weak")
strong <- invariance_fit("strong")
```

Passing several fits to `anova()` compares them as nested models, which is how
you test whether a stricter level of invariance is tenable. Alongside the
chi-square difference test it reports each model's own `RMSEA` and `CFI` and
the change in each from the previous model. A difference test rejects almost
any constraint in a large enough sample, so invariance is conventionally judged
on those changes as well. `indices` takes any measure `lavaan::fitMeasures()`
knows, in the order you want the columns: `indices = c("rmsea", "cfi", "srmr")`,
or `NULL` for none. (lavaan's `RMSEA_D` column is a third thing again: the
RMSEA of the difference test itself.)

```{r invariance-compare}
anova(configural, weak, strong)
```

`invariance_between` does the same across groups in a multigroup model.

Identification is handled for you, including a case that is easy to get wrong:
a construct measured at a **single** occasion by exactly **two** indicators
needs both loadings fixed to 1 and both intercepts fixed to 0. Partial fixing
(the usual referent-indicator or effects-coding scheme) leaves it
under-identified. `identification_scheme()` is the function that decides:

```{r identification}
identification_scheme(n_occasions = 1, n_indicators = 2, lv_scaling = "effect")
identification_scheme(n_occasions = 6, n_indicators = 2, lv_scaling = "effect")
```

# Residual structure

With a latent dependent variable measured repeatedly, the same indicator's
residuals usually correlate over occasions, and their variances may be worth
constraining. Both are described with `resid_set()`, which says *which*
residual terms a constraint covers: the indicators, and the conditions.

`resid_cov` adds residual covariances among a set's members. Name an indicator
and it covers every occasion:

```{r resid-cov}
fit_rescov <- semnova(
    data = reading_two,
    id = "id",
    dv = "dv",
    indicator = "indicator",
    withins = c("grade", "sentence"),
    resid_cov = resid_set("fix_count"),
    contrasts_arg = list(grade = "contr.sum", sentence = "contr.sum")
)

anova(fit_latent, fit_rescov)
```

Covariances in a set are free by default; `equal = TRUE` makes them one
parameter. Conditions restrict the set to part of the design. Here it covers
residual covariances among landolt sentences only, constrained equal:

```{r resid-cov-conditions}
fit_landolt <- semnova(
    data = reading_two,
    id = "id",
    dv = "dv",
    indicator = "indicator",
    withins = c("grade", "sentence"),
    resid_cov = resid_set("fix_count", sentence = "landolt", equal = TRUE),
    contrasts_arg = list(grade = "contr.sum", sentence = "contr.sum")
)

fit_measures(fit_landolt)
```

`resid_var` uses the same sets to constrain residual *variances* to be equal.
Omit the indicator and the set covers all of them; `TRUE` is shorthand for one
set covering everything:

```{r resid-var}
equal_over_time <- semnova(
    data = reading_two,
    id = "id",
    dv = "dv",
    indicator = "indicator",
    withins = c("grade", "sentence"),
    # each indicator's residual variance held constant across occasions
    resid_var = list(resid_set("fix_count"), resid_set("ini_land_pos")),
    contrasts_arg = list(grade = "contr.sum", sentence = "contr.sum")
)

anova(fit_latent, equal_over_time)
```

A set is printed the way you wrote it, and is checked as you write it rather
than deep inside the fit:

```{r resid-set-print}
resid_set("fix_count", sentence = "landolt", equal = TRUE)
try(resid_set("fix_count", grade = "grade7"))
```

Two cases where a residual constraint cannot apply, both warned about rather
than silently dropped: a **manifest** dependent variable has no residuals of its
own (the observed variable is the construct), and a set covering fewer than two
residual terms, which happens with a single occasion, has nothing to
constrain.

`build_resid_cov_syntax()` and `build_resid_var_syntax()` write this part of
the model, if you want the syntax itself.

```{r resid-syntax}
cat(build_resid_var_syntax(list(c("Y1", "Y2", "Y3"))))
```

# The covariance structure of the contrast variables

By default the contrast variables have an unstructured covariance matrix: every
variance and covariance is freely estimated, and the model is saturated. Two
options impose the classical repeated-measures structures instead.

`sphericity` constrains a model term's contrast variables to equal variances and
zero covariances among themselves. That is the assumption a classical RM-ANOVA
makes, stated explicitly here and therefore testable. You name the terms, in the same
vocabulary as the ANOVA table: `TRUE` for every term wide enough to constrain,
or particular terms such as `"grade"` and `"grade:sentence"` (an interaction may
also be given as its factors, `c("grade", "sentence")`).

```{r sphericity}
fit_spher <- semnova(
    data = reading_manifest,
    id = "id",
    dv = "re_fix_time",
    withins = c("grade", "sentence"),
    sphericity = TRUE,
    contrasts_arg = list(grade = "contr.sum", sentence = "contr.sum")
)

fit_measures(fit_spher)
```

Because the sphericity model is nested in the unstructured one, `anova()` tests
the assumption directly:

```{r sphericity-test}
anova(fit, fit_spher)
```

`compound_symmetry` puts the structure on the occasions instead: one variance
for every occasion and one covariance for every pair, with the contrast
variables' own (co)variances fixed to zero.

```{r compound-symmetry}
fit_cs <- semnova(
    data = reading_manifest,
    id = "id",
    dv = "re_fix_time",
    withins = c("grade", "sentence"),
    compound_symmetry = TRUE,
    contrasts_arg = list(grade = "contr.sum", sentence = "contr.sum")
)

anova(fit, fit_cs)
```

In a multigroup model, `variance_homogeneity = TRUE` constrains those
(co)variances to be equal across groups, and `group_weights = "stochastic"`
treats group membership as random rather than fixed by design. Each group's
frequency is then estimated and reported as a `relfreq` definition.

```{r group-weights}
fit_weighted <- semnova(
    data = reading_manifest,
    id = "id",
    dv = "re_fix_time",
    withins = c("grade", "sentence"),
    betweens = "sex",
    group_weights = "stochastic",
    variance_homogeneity = TRUE,
    contrasts_arg = list(
        grade = "contr.sum", sentence = "contr.sum", sex = "contr.treatment"
    )
)

estimates <- lavaan::parTable(fit_weighted$sem_obj)
estimates[estimates$op == ":=", c("lhs", "est")]
```

`build_pi_layer_syntax()` and `build_group_weight_syntax()` are the functions
that write this part of the model, should you want the syntax itself.

```{r structure-syntax}
cat(build_group_weight_syntax(c("m", "w"), "stochastic"))
```

# Hypothesis tests

Every row of the ANOVA table is a hypothesis, and every hypothesis can be
inspected on its own. `test_hypothesis()` returns both the individual contrast
estimates and the omnibus test.

```{r hypotheses}
term_names <- vapply(fit$hypotheses, function(h) h$description, character(1))
term_names

grade_effect <- fit$hypotheses[[which(term_names == "grade")]]
test_hypothesis(fit, grade_effect)
```

`contrast_estimates()` is the same function under a name that describes the
other half of what it returns; use whichever reads better at the call site.
`sd_between` is the between-person standard deviation of the effect. It says
how much the effect varies across people, not how precisely it is estimated.

```{r contrast-estimates}
contrast_estimates(fit, grade_effect, level = 0.99)$table
```

`contrast_table()` stacks the estimates for every term at once.

```{r contrast-table}
contrast_table(fit)
```

## Custom hypotheses

You are not limited to the terms of the design. Build any general linear
hypothesis with `hypothesis()` and pass it to the same function. There is no
separate code path for custom tests.

A hypothesis is specified by up to four matrices: `M` picks out
within-subject contrasts, `G` group contrasts, `L` covariate contrasts, and `K`
the value tested against (zero by default). Any of them may be omitted when the
design makes them unnecessary.

Here we test a single within-subject contrast on its own:

```{r custom-hypothesis}
M <- matrix(0, nrow = length(fit$pis), ncol = 1)
M[2, 1] <- 1

my_hypothesis <- hypothesis(M = M, description = "second contrast only")
test_hypothesis(fit, my_hypothesis)
```

`validate_hypothesis()` checks a hypothesis against a fit and fills in whatever
can be defaulted, which is useful when building hypotheses programmatically:

```{r validate-hypothesis}
validate_hypothesis(my_hypothesis, fit)
dim(my_hypothesis$K)
```

# Plots

`plot()` visualises one term's contrast estimates. Name the term with `terms=`
(order does not matter) or pass a hypothesis object directly.

```{r plot-ci}
plot(fit, terms = c("grade", "sentence"), interval = "ci")
```

Switching `interval` to `"sd"` shows between-person variability instead of the
confidence interval. It shows the spread of the effect across people.

```{r plot-sd}
plot(fit, terms = "grade", interval = "sd", geom = c("point", "line"))
```

`dag()` draws the model as a SEM path diagram, laid out in the structure a
semnova model has: residual terms, then indicators, then the latent variables
they measure, then the contrast variables, then any covariates.

Standard SEM conventions apply. Single-headed arrows are directed effects
(loadings, regressions); double-headed arrows and self-loops are
(co)variances. Squares are manifest variables, circles latent ones, triangles
the constant. Fixed parameters are marked with a ring accent over the estimate.

By default the diagram shows the measurement and regression structure. That is the
part you usually want to see. A fully crossed design has a great many
(co)variances, so drawing everything at once is rarely readable.

```{r dag, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 9}
dag(fit_cov)
```

`what` controls which parts are drawn. Give any of `"measurement"`,
`"regression"`, `"variance"`, `"covariance"`, `"resid_var"`, `"resid_cov"`,
`"intercept"`, or `"all"`. Residual variances appear as their own epsilon
nodes, and intercepts as triangles:

```{r dag-all, fig.height = 7.5, fig.width = 10}
dag(fit_cov, what = c("measurement", "regression", "resid_var", "variance"))
```

Multigroup fits are drawn as facets, one panel per group, labelled with the
group name:

```{r dag-groups, fig.height = 5, fig.width = 10}
dag(fit_between)
```

`labels` controls the estimates: `"all"` (the default) labels every parameter
drawn. Fixed ones, such as the contrast loadings, are shown inside a ring
accent, so design and estimate stay distinguishable. `"free"` labels only freely
estimated parameters, which thins out a dense diagram; `"none"` gives a bare
structural one.

If a dense model looks cluttered, `x_scale` and `y_scale` stretch the node
positions horizontally and vertically. Only their ratio matters, because
stretching both equally gives the same diagram. The tighter direction keeps its
spacing and the other grows away from it. Here the columns are pushed apart while the
rows stay as they were:

```{r dag-scale, fig.height = 8.1, fig.width = 12.9}
p <- dag(fit_cov, x_scale = 1.5)
attr(p, "fig_size") # the figure size this needs, in inches
p
```

A scaled diagram is drawn at a physical size rather than fitted to the figure,
so it needs a figure big enough to hold it. That is what the `fig_size`
attribute is for, and the chunk options above were set from it. Unscaled, `dag()` fits
whatever figure it is given, and a bigger `fig.width`/`fig.height` is the
simplest cure for crowding.

The curved paths, meaning variance self-loops and covariance arcs, are drawn
at a fixed size and a fixed bend angle. so scaling the layout or resizing the figure
leaves them alone. `curve_scale` is what changes them, with `variance_scale`
and `covariance_scale` following it unless you set them yourself:

```{r dag-curve, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 12}
dag(fit_between, what = c("measurement", "regression", "variance", "covariance"),
    curve_scale = 1.6)
```

A scaled diagram is fitted to the figure rather than cropped by it: if the
figure is smaller than `fig_size`, you get a smaller diagram, not a piece of
one. Since the markers and text keep their fixed size, though, a figure well
under `fig_size` will crowd again. Scaling sets the shape, the figure gives
the room.

`dag_save()` writes a diagram to a file and crops the whitespace off it. There
is always some: the layout is fitted to the figure, and the margins have to be
wide enough for the labels that overhang the panel. Dimensions default to the
plot's own `fig_size`.

```{r dag-save}
cropped <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
plain <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")

dag_save(cropped, dag(fit_cov), dpi = 100)
dag_save(plain, dag(fit_cov), dpi = 100, trim = FALSE)

vapply(c(cropped = cropped, uncropped = plain), file.size, numeric(1))
```

Cropping needs the `magick` package and a raster format; without either the
file is still written, uncropped, with a message saying why. `padding` sets the
margin left around the diagram, in pixels.

# Looking inside a fit

`model_parameters()` is the single canonical read of a fitted model: every
parameter, classified by type.

```{r model-parameters}
params <- model_parameters(fit_cov)
table(params$type)

head(model_parameters(fit_cov, what = "regression")[c("lhs", "rhs", "est", "se", "type")])
```

`regression_coefficients()` reshapes those into the arrays the contrast machinery
uses: the coefficients, their sampling covariance, and the between-person
covariance of the contrast variables.

```{r regression-coefficients}
coefs <- regression_coefficients(fit_cov)
dim(coefs$B_array)
dimnames(coefs$B_array)[["covariate"]]
```

The underlying `lavaan` fit is always available if you need something the
package does not expose:

```{r sem-obj}
class(fit_cov$sem_obj)
```

# The lower-level interface

`semnova()` derives the latent variables and contrast matrix from your design.
When you want to specify them yourself, for a contrast matrix no standard
contrast function produces, use `lgc()` directly.

You supply data in wide format, the constructs and their indicators, and the
contrast matrix.

```{r lgc}
wide <- fit$data
custom_contrasts <- solve(cbind(1, stats::contr.poly(6)))

fit_lgc <- lgc(
    data = wide,
    etas = fit$etas_mmodel,
    c_matrix_within = custom_contrasts,
    hypotheses = hypothesis(M = M, description = "custom contrast")
)

anova_table(fit_lgc)
```

Everything shown above works the same way on an `lgc()` fit. The ANOVA-style
interface is a convenience layer, not a separate model.

# Building blocks

The syntax generators `semnova()` calls are exported too, for anyone who wants
to inspect or reuse the generated `lavaan` syntax. `build_measurement_syntax()`
writes the measurement model:

```{r syntax-measurement}
etas <- list(eta1 = c("Y1", "Y2", "Y3"))
cat(build_measurement_syntax(etas, lv_scaling = "effect"))
```

`build_pi_layer_syntax()` writes the contrast layer, `build_covariate_syntax()`
the covariate model and its regressions, and `build_resid_cov_syntax()` any
residual covariances you want to allow:

```{r syntax-others}
cat(build_pi_layer_syntax(matrix(c(1, 1, 1, -1), nrow = 2), eta_names = c("eta1", "eta2")))

cat(build_resid_cov_syntax(equal_resid_cov = list(c("Y1", "Y2", "Y3"))))
```

`strip_construct_structure()` removes a construct's own mean and variance lines,
which is what lets the measurement model and the contrast layer be combined
without specifying the same parameter twice:

```{r strip}
cat(strip_construct_structure("eta1 =~ Y1\neta1 ~~ eta1\neta1 ~ 1", "eta1"))
```

`parse_design()` turns factor columns into the contrast matrices a design
implies, and `generate_anova_hypotheses()` crosses two designs into one
hypothesis per model term:

```{r parse-design}
within_design <- parse_design(
    reading_manifest,
    factors = c("grade", "sentence"),
    contrasts_arg = list(grade = "contr.sum", sentence = "contr.sum")
)
within_design$effect_names
round(within_design$c_matrix, 3)
```

`contrast_matrix()` builds the Kronecker contrast matrix behind every test:

```{r contrast-matrix}
R <- contrast_matrix(G = matrix(1), L = matrix(1), M = M)
dim(R$R)
```

# Parameter names

Parameters carry structured labels, generated and read back by one small set of
functions so that writing the model and reading its results can never disagree.

A parameter's identity is its type and its indices, and every rendering comes
from those: the lavaan label the model is written with, a readable text form,
and the plotmath `dag()` draws on the arrows.

```{r param-names}
param_label("regression", pi = 2, covariate = 1, group = 1)
param_label("regression", pi = 2, covariate = 1, group = 1, format = "text")
param_label("regression", pi = 2, covariate = 1, group = 1, format = "plotmath")
parse_param_label(".beta_2_1_1")
```

The labels also state their **equality constraints**. Every parameter of the
measurement model is labelled by the same engine. An index of `0`, shown as
`*`, means "one parameter across this whole dimension". Under strong
within-invariance the six occasions share one loading per indicator, and the
label says so:

```{r param-invariance}
labels <- lavaan::parTable(fit_latent$sem_obj)$label
loadings <- unique(grep("^\\.lambda_", labels, value = TRUE))
loadings
pretty_label(loadings[1], format = "text") # * = shared across occasions
```

`pretty_label()` is for labels you already have as a string, such as those read
off a fitted model; prefer `param_label(format = )` whenever you know the
parameter's identity.

`regression_labels()` enumerates one family as a positioned array: the pi-layer
regression coefficients, `(covariate x pi x group)`. That is the array
`regression_coefficients()` fills with estimates, and the two come from the same
call so they cannot drift apart. Everything else in the model is named one label
at a time, where it is written.

```{r param-labels}
regression_labels(pis = 1:2, covariates = "iq", groups = "1")[, , 1]
```

`n_occasions()` reports how many occasions a construct is measured at. The
identification rules depend on that count.

```{r n-occasions}
n_occasions("iq", n_within_occasions = 6, covariate_names = "iq")
```

# What is not here yet

These are known gaps rather than oversights:

- **Power analysis**. Deferred. It will return in a later release.
- **Marginal effects**. The old `Effect()` method is not carried over. Use
  `plot()` on a hypothesis instead.

```{r session}
sessionInfo()
```
